extracted.intended_audience: appellate judges, administrative-law practitioners, Supreme Court justices, and administrative-law scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative considerations for determining whether Chevron deference (and similar judicial deference to agency statutory interpretations) should be retained, applied, or overruled, viewed through stare decisis, statutory text/APA, and practical effects. Emphasizes historical practice, coherence with surrounding law, workability, and reliance consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron deference is inconsistent with the APA's directions (including 5 U.S.C. §706) and cannot be reconciled with the APA's commands simply because scholars or agencies prefer it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a judicially created rule of deference conflicts with statutory commands in the APA; do not accept academic or agency views as substitutes for statutory text. Example: authorities acknowledging Chevron 'seems in conflict with ... language of 706.' Anti-pattern: treating scholarly endorsements or agency practice as dispositive against clear APA directives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis Lesson 1 — Judicial humility to the written law
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges must exercise independent judgment and yield to the laws adopted by the people's elected representatives; judicial humility demands fidelity to written law rather than substituting agency views for the best reading of statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether continuing to apply a precedent would require judges to abandon independent adjudication in favor of deferring to current executive interpretations. Scoring note: greater weight when precedent forces courts to 'abandon the best reading of the law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis Lesson 2 — Precedent test: endorsement, coherence, and survival
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedents that have 'won the endorsement of judges across many generations, demonstrated coherence with our broader law, and weathered the tests of time and experience are entitled to greater consideration' when deciding whether to retain or overrule them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a precedent by (a) breadth and longevity of judicial endorsement, (b) coherence with surrounding law and constitutional structure, and (c) whether it has withstood time and practical application. Anti-pattern: treating a recent or idiosyncratic decision as a settled doctrine deserving full stare decisis protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful consideration vs. binding deference to executive constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: While courts may give 'great respect' to contemporaneous and consistent executive constructions, they are not 'bound' by all reasonable administrative constructions; respect differs from judicially compelled deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between giving weight to agency interpretations (Skidmore-like consideration) versus mandatory deference that displaces judicial interpretation. Guidance: consider thoroughness, validity of reasoning, consistency, and persuasive power rather than automatic binding effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with Article III judicial role and separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron-type deference can 'preclude courts from exercising the judicial power vested in them by Article III' by forcing courts to accept executive views instead of saying what the law is, undermining judicial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a doctrine transfers core judicial functions to the Executive, thereby tilting adjudication in favor of the government and undermining impartial adjudication. Example harms: agencies effectively judging their own authority (Arlington v. FCC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict with due process and nemo iudex (no one judge in their own case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing agencies to determine the scope of their own powers risks violating due process principles that no person should be a judge in their own case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether deference permits the agency to act as judge, party, and beneficiary, creating procedural fairness problems. Use as a constitutional check when agency self‑adjudication affects individual rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textualism and fair-notice concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts traditionally construe statutes 'as a reasonable reader would when the law was made' (textualism); a deferential, fluid approach undermines fair notice and due process because individuals cannot be sure of the rules that bind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a doctrine's compatibility with focusing on statutory text, linguistic context, and canons of construction. Anti-pattern: allowing recurring executive reinterpretation to replace statutory clarity, creating unpredictability for regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of lenity and penal-construction protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron deference can displace the rule of lenity, which requires ambiguities in penal statutes be resolved against the government, thereby weakening protections for individual liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criminal or punitive consequences are at stake, prefer interpretive rules (like lenity) that protect liberty over deferential doctrines that empower administrative punishment based on ambiguous statutory readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workability of Chevron (indeterminacy of steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron's multi-step regime (including 'step zero' / Mead, step one ambiguity inquiry, and step two reasonableness review) has proved indeterminate in application; courts disagree about when and how to apply each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a precedent by whether its doctrinal framework yields clear, consistent application. Problems to note: lack of consensus on when delegation exists (Mead factors), when a statute is 'ambiguous' at step one, and what 'reasonable' review requires at step two. Anti-pattern: flexible multi-step rules that produce 'wildly different' outcomes across courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mead / 'step zero' delegation inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying Chevron, courts may need to determine whether Congress intended to delegate interpretive authority to the agency (Mead multifactor test), but that inquiry itself is indeterminate and has been applied inconsistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a judicially inferred delegation is justified by statutory text or by clear congressional intent; be wary of treating implied delegation as a default. Example: Mead's multifactor test has produced inconsistent results and is sometimes ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron step one — ambiguity determination
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one a judge must decide whether the statute is 'ambiguous' as to the precise question; courts and litigants lack a stable criterion for spotting such ambiguity, producing inconsistent findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require a principled, text-and-structure-based analysis to label an issue 'ambiguous'; avoid ad hoc or novelty-based 'snark hunt' for ambiguity. Scoring note: overbroad or underinclusive identifications of ambiguity undermine coherent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron step two — reasonableness review
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two a court assesses whether the agency's interpretation of an ambiguous statute is 'reasonable', but courts vary widely in how searching that review should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether the review is searching or highly deferential, and ground the standard in textual and structural reasoning. Anti-pattern: reflexive acceptance of agency labels as 'reasonable' without independent statutory analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance interests and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine that permits agencies to replace one 'reasonable' interpretation with another at will undermines reliance interests and legal predictability, harming ordinary people who cannot track or influence administrative shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how a rule affects settled expectations and retrospective or prospective reliance. Example harms: Brand X (oscillating internet-regulation definitions), Buffington (veteran's withheld benefits), De Niz Robles (immigration retrospective effects). Give special weight where individuals (vs. sophisticated actors) are disadvantaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional fairness and power imbalance
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron deference systematically biases outcomes in favor of the most powerful litigant — the federal government — and benefits sophisticated actors who can influence or follow agency shifts, whereas ordinary people suffer disproportionate harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a doctrine, analyze who bears the costs of doctrinal uncertainty. Anti-pattern: treating doctrine as neutral when its practical effects concentrate advantage with government or regulated elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore factors for persuasive weight
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency's interpretation is not controlling, the weight due that interpretation 'depends upon' the thoroughness of the agency's consideration, validity of reasoning, consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and other persuasive factors (Skidmore).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Skidmore-style multi-factor persuasion analysis (thoroughness, reasoning, consistency, persuasive power) rather than automatic coercive deference. Scoring guidance: well-reasoned, consistent, and thoroughly explained agency interpretations merit greater weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'power quoting' — don't elevate stray passages beyond their context
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not endow stray or isolated passages in prior decisions with extraordinary authority; beware of a single line being treated as the anchor for a sweeping doctrinal revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the full context and reasoning of prior decisions before importing any passage as precedent for a broad rule. Anti-pattern: basing a new binding doctrine on a brief, non-adversarial, or context-lacking formulation in an earlier decision (as argued about Chevron's origins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with other traditional presumptions and canons
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive presumptions and canons (e.g., federalism canon, presumption against retroactivity, contra proferentem, lenity) embody longstanding constitutional and jurisprudential commitments; a deference doctrine should be measured for consonance with these canons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether adopting or retaining a doctrine would invert or undermine longstanding canons that protect constitutional structure or individual rights. Example: Chevron cannot claim the centuries-old pedigree of traditional canons and often works contrary to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence of judicial practice and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: History demonstrates courts before Chevron resolved complex, technical statutory disputes without mandatory deference; recent practice shows the Court can resolve technical issues by text, context, and structure alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether empirical experience supports the necessity of a deferential rule for handling technical matters. Anti-pattern: assuming courts cannot resolve technical questions without agency deference when the record shows otherwise (cases like Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation; Sackett v. EPA; Johnson v. Guzman Chavez).
